title: The Pitfall of Scaling Up: Uncovering and Mitigating Popularity Bias Amplification in Scaling Transformer-based Recommenders

paper.title: The Pitfall of Scaling Up: Uncovering and Mitigating Popularity Bias Amplification in Scaling Transformer-based Recommenders
paper.abstract: Abstract. We identify a critical pitfall in scaling transformer-based sequential recommenders: while increasing model size improves recommendation accuracy, it simultaneously amplifies popularity bias . This bias drives systems to over-recommend popular items at the expense of niche ones, which not only undermines fairness but also degrades the broader ecosystem by reinforcing the Matthew effect and filter bubbles. Consequently, this bias amplification emerges as a fundamental obstacle to sustainable model scaling. Through comprehensive theoretical and empirical analyses, we uncover the root cause of this amplification. Our findings reveal that as model depth increases, the two core components of the transformer architecture, i.e., attention aggregation and feed-forward projections, synergistically induce severe spectral collapse in model predictions, which directly translates to the amplification of popularity bias. To address this challenge, we propose SPRINT ( S calable P opularity R egularization IN T ransformers), which mitigates spectral collapse during scaling by constraining (i) the maximum column-sums of the attention score matrices and (ii) the spectral norms of the feed-forward parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPRINT significantly improves both accuracy and long-tail fairness. Crucially, it yields more favorable scaling behaviors when expanding model sizes from 0.05M to 0.34B parameters. The code is available at https://github.com/Tiny-Snow/GenRec .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: The discovery of scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of modern machine learning. These laws characterize a remarkable empirical regularity: model performance improves predictably (often following a power law) as the number of parameters or the volume of data increases ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022a ) . Guided by these observations, transformer-based foundation models have been scaled to billions or even trillions of parameters ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025a ) , unlocking unprecedented proficiency in contextual understanding ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Hao et al., 2025 ) , complex reasoning ( Wei et al., 2022b ; Wang et al., 2025c ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , and agency ( Hao et al., 2026a ; Hao et al., 2026b ) . Inspired by this success, researchers have increasingly explored scaling laws in recommender systems, particularly in sequential recommendation ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Recent studies have observed a similar trend: scaling up the parameters of transformer-based sequential recommenders leads to consistent improvements in recommendation accuracy, which has also been validated in large-scale industrial recommender systems ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zivic et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . Movielens-20M scaling laws. Figure 1 . Scaling laws of accuracy (NDCG@5) and fairness (Fair-0.95) on transformer-based sequential recommenders, across (1) different number of non-embedding parameters (0.05M to 0.34B) and (2) different transformer depths (1 to 16 layers). Here we present results on the MovieLens-20M dataset ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) with the advanced SASRec++ backbone ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) , and the fairness metric denotes the ratio of bottom-95% long-tail items exposed in top-1 recommendations. Notably, as model size increases, especially by deepening layers, fairness tends to degrade due to amplified popularity bias. Our proposed SPRINT effectively mitigates this bias, enabling superior scaling performance in both accuracy and fairness. Movielens-20M scaling laws. Challenge. However, we uncover a critical pitfall of scaling sequential recommenders: as model size increases, especially when increasing transformer depth, popularity bias is simultaneously amplified, as shown in Figure 1 . Popularity bias ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) , a notorious issue in recommender systems, denotes the tendency to over-recommend popular items at the expense of niche ones. This bias adversely affects both accuracy and fairness and can further degrade the recommendation ecosystem by reinforcing the Matthew effect and intensifying filter bubbles through the user-system feedback loop ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . The severity of these consequences poses a fundamental challenge to achieving sustainable scaling in recommendation. Analysis. To tackle this challenge, we first conduct theoretical and empirical analyses to pinpoint the root cause behind the amplification of popularity bias during model scaling. Prior work by Lin et al. (2025) indicates that item popularity is primarily encoded within the principal spectral component of the model’s prediction score matrix, which is weighted by the largest singular value ( i.e., the spectral norm) in the singular value decomposition ( cf. Lemma 3.1 ). Based on this insight, we further empirically observe that increasing transformer depth exacerbates spectral collapse ( Jing et al., 2021 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Ohsaka and Togashi, 2023 ) : the largest singular value grows disproportionately dominant relative to the rest of the singular values, thereby magnifying the influence of the popularity-related principal component on final recommendations, and consequently amplifying popularity bias as model scales up ( cf. Figure 1 ). Diving deeper into the architectural mechanisms, we attribute the aforementioned depth-induced spectral collapse to the two core components of transformer-based sequential recommenders: attention aggregation and feed-forward projections . Specifically, the attention mechanism can over-emphasize popular items as they tend to accumulate disproportionately high attention weights. Our theoretical analysis further shows that stacking layers with such popularity-priority attention intensifies spectral collapse by increasing the spectral norm exponentially with depth ( cf. Theorem 3.2 ). Moreover, the gradient dynamics of stacked feed-forward projections can make gradient-based optimization less effective in learning features within the long-tail singular space, further exacerbating spectral collapse as the network deepens ( cf. Lemma 3.3 ). Together, these two mechanisms synergistically amplify popularity bias and impede the scalability of sequential recommenders. Our Method. Given the adverse impact of popularity bias on the fairness and sustainability of recommendation systems, developing effective debiasing strategies is crucial. While numerous debiasing methods have been proposed ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Zhang and Shen, 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ; Ning et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Lin et al., 2025 ) , most primarily target traditional collaborative filtering scenarios, overlooking the unique characteristics of sequential recommendation and the implications of model architectures on scaling laws. Consequently, these approaches are less effective in addressing the popularity bias amplification observed during scaling. To bridge this gap, we propose SPRINT , a popularity regularization method tailored to transformer-based sequential recommenders. Motivated by our prior theoretical analysis, SPRINT introduces two key regularizers: (i) attention regularization , which constrains the maximum column-sums of the attention score matrices, limiting the excessive accumulation of popularity signals during attention aggregation, thus mitigating popularity bias amplification; and (ii) feed-forward regularization , which bounds the spectral norms of the feed-forward projection weights, thereby controlling spectral collapse as depth increases. By regularizing these core components in each layer, SPRINT can natively alleviate spectral collapse when training deeper transformers. SPRINT offers three appealing properties: (i) We prove that SPRINT upper-bounds the spectral norm of the prediction score matrix, providing theoretical guarantees for mitigating popularity bias amplification ( cf. Theorem 4.1 ). (ii) Unlike existing debiasing approaches, SPRINT directly targets the architectural sources of this amplification by regularizing the specific transformer components. (iii) SPRINT is computationally efficient, introducing negligible training overhead. These properties make SPRINT a principled and effective debiasing solution for scaling sequential recommenders. We evaluate SPRINT on six benchmark datasets using two strong sequential recommendation backbones: SASRec++ ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) and HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) . Experimental results demonstrate that SPRINT significantly improves both accuracy (avg. +15.70% in NDCG and HR) and long-tail exposure (avg. +7.12%). To assess scalability, we test model sizes ranging from 0.05M to 0.34B non-embedding parameters (a 6912 × \times scale-up). The results show that SPRINT achieves better accuracy scaling while maintaining a more balanced popularity distribution ( cf. Figure 1 ). We further extend SPRINT to the generative recommendation scenario and observe consistent gains on the state-of-the-art backbones TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) and LETTER ( Wang et al., 2024c ) . Our Contributions • We identify a critical scaling pitfall in sequential recommendation: while accuracy improves with model scaling, popularity bias is simultaneously amplified. • We reveal that attention aggregation and feed-forward projections in transformer synergistically exacerbate the spectral collapse of model predictions, thereby intensifying popularity bias as depth grows. • We propose SPRINT, a principled and effective popularity regularization method that constrains the maximum column-sums of the attention matrices and the spectral norms of feed-forward parameters to mitigate this spectral collapse. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPRINT significantly improves both accuracy and fairness ( i.e., long-tail exposure), yielding more favorable scaling behaviors.

sections.heading: 2. Preliminaries
sections.text: In this section, we formulate the sequential recommendation task in Section 2.1 , introduce the popularity bias in Section 2.2 , and present the transformer-based model architectures in Section 2.3 .

sections.heading: 2.1. Task Formulation
sections.text: In this work, we focus on sequential recommendation ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2026a ; Cui et al., 2026b ) , a widely adopted paradigm in real-world recommender systems. Formally, given a set of users 𝒰 \mathcal{U} and a set of items ℐ \mathcal{I} , each user u ∈ 𝒰 u\in\mathcal{U} interacts with a sequence of items ( i u , 1 , i u , 2 , ⋯ , i u , n u ) (i_{u,1},i_{u,2},\cdots,i_{u,n_{u}}) in chronological order. Here, i u , t ∈ ℐ i_{u,t}\in\mathcal{I} denotes the t t -th item the user interacts with, and n u n_{u} represents the length of the interaction sequence. Given this historical sequence as input, the goal of a sequential recommendation model is to predict the next item i u , n u + 1 i_{u,n_{u}+1} that the user is most likely to interact with.

sections.heading: 2.2. Popularity Bias
sections.text: Recommender systems often exhibit a long-tail distribution of item popularity, where a small fraction of items ( i.e., popular items ) receive a disproportionately large number of interactions, while the majority of items ( i.e., long-tail items ) are rarely interacted with ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . For instance, in the ML-1M dataset ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) , the top-20% of items (ranked by popularity) account for 62.6% of all interactions, while the bottom-40% account for only 5.4%. Such a skewed data distribution poses significant challenges for training effective recommendation models, as these models often amplify this skewness by over-recommending popular items. For example, when employing the state-of-the-art HSTU model ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) on ML-1M, we observe that over 80% of the recommendations are dominated by the top-20% popular items, whereas the bottom-40% long-tail items are recommended less than 1% of the time. This notorious phenomenon, known as popularity bias , not only hinders recommendation accuracy but also leads to information cocoons, inequitable exposure, and reduced user satisfaction ( Zhu et al., 2021 ; Klimashevskaia et al., 2024 ) . To quantify the extent of popularity bias in recommendation systems, we additionally measure a fairness metric Fair- α \alpha , defined as the ratio of bottom- α \alpha long-tail items in the final recommendations, which is also referred to as the long-tail exposure. Following prior work ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate Fair-0.8 by treating the bottom 80% of items as long-tail items across most datasets ( cf. Table 1 ). For the ML-20M dataset, due to its massive scale and particularly skewed popularity distribution, we instead evaluate Fair-0.95 ( cf. Figure 1 ). In the main text, we primarily evaluate fairness in top-1 recommendations, while the similar trends can be observed in top-5 and top-10 recommendations ( cf. Table 8 ).

sections.heading: 3. Pitfalls of Scaling Laws
sections.text: In this section, we identify a critical pitfall in scaling sequential recommendation models: while scaling up model size generally enhances performance, it simultaneously amplifies popularity bias . We first provide empirical evidence in Section 3.1 , then conduct empirical and theoretical analyses of the root causes in Section 3.2 .

sections.heading: 3.1. Popularity Bias Amplification
sections.text: Motivated by recent efforts to scale sequential recommendation models ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zivic et al., 2024 ) , we conduct an empirical study to investigate the impact of model size on both recommendation accuracy and fairness. As shown in Figure 1 .(1), our results reveal an intriguing pattern: while overall recommendation accuracy improves with larger model sizes, recommendation fairness exhibits a non-monotonic trajectory. Specifically, popularity bias decreases as model size grows to a moderate scale ( e.g., 18.9M), likely due to an enhanced capacity to align with user preferences. However, when further scaling to large sizes ( e.g., 0.13B and 0.34B), popularity bias significantly worsens, suggesting an increased tendency to over-recommend popular items and underutilize long-tail features. More crucially, this popularity bias is continuously amplified as model depth increases, eventually becoming a bottleneck to further scaling. In Figure 1 .(2), we observe accuracy saturation, and in some cases even degradation, when model depth is increased ( e.g., over 8 layers) without additional debiasing mechanisms. Overall, these findings reveal a critical pitfall in scaling sequential recommenders: Observation: Popularity Bias Pitfall in Scaling When scaling model size, particularly by increasing model depth, popularity bias is simultaneously amplified and can become a bottleneck to further scaling.

The feed-forward projection can be viewed as a product of multiple weight matrices, serving to effectively capture generalizable patterns in the representation space. sections.heading: 4. Methodology
sections.text: Given the aforementioned concerns regarding popularity bias amplification during model scaling, as well as the underlying causes rooted in spectral collapse from stacking attention and feed-forward layers, blindly scaling up sequential recommenders without constraining spectral norm growth will almost inevitably lead to sub-optimal scalability. Motivated by this critical pitfall, we propose SPRINT ( S calable P opularity R egularization IN T ransformers), a principled approach that explicitly bounds the spectral norm within key transformer components to mitigate bias amplification and unlock sustainable scalability. In the following, we first present the algorithmic details of SPRINT in Section 4.1 , and subsequently provide theoretical analyses and comparative discussions in Section 4.2 .

sections.heading: 4.1. Scalable Popularity Regularization
sections.text: Recognizing spectral collapse in deep sequential recommenders as the root cause of popularity bias amplification, our approach tries to address this issue by directly constraining the spectral norm within the transformer components of each layer. Specifically, our proposed SPRINT introduces two regularization terms: attention regularization and feed-forward regularization . Attention Regularization. As Theorem 3.2 reveals, stacking multiple attention layers with similar spectral patterns ( e.g., prioritizing high-popularity items) inevitably drives exponential growth in the spectral norm. A natural solution to alleviate this effect is to explicitly restrict the spectral norm of the attention score matrix 𝐒 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{S}^{(\ell)} at each layer ℓ \ell , thereby upper-bounding the spectral norm of the entire attention aggregation: (4.1) ∥ 𝐒 ( L ) 𝐒 ( L − 1 ) ⋯ 𝐒 ( 1 ) ∥ 2 ≤ ∏ ℓ = 1 L ∥ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ∥ 2 . \|\mathbf{S}^{(L)}\mathbf{S}^{(L-1)}\cdots\mathbf{S}^{(1)}\|_{2}\leq\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}. However, directly optimizing ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{2} is highly non-trivial. Computing the exact spectral norm of this N × N N\times N matrix requires expensive SVD operations with a time complexity of O ⁡ ( | 𝒰 | ​ n ¯ 3 ) O(|\mathcal{U}|\bar{n}^{3}) , which is practically infeasible for large-scale recommendation models. Furthermore, while power iteration methods ( Golub and Van Loan, 2013 ; Golub and Van der Vorst, 2000 ; Yoshida and Miyato, 2017 ) can approximate the spectral norm of static parameter weights in quadratic time, they are inapplicable to attention scores, as these matrices are input-dependent and evolve drastically during training. Instead, we optimize a computationally tractable surrogate upper bound for the spectral norm by leveraging the desirable row-normalized properties of attention matrices: (4.2) ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 ≤ ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ 1 ⋅ ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ ∞ = ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ 1 , \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{\|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{1}\cdot\|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{\infty}}=\sqrt{\|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{1}}, where ∥ ⋅ ∥ 1 \|\cdot\|_{1} and ∥ ⋅ ∥ ∞ \|\cdot\|_{\infty} denote the matrix 1-norm ( i.e., maximum absolute column sum) and infinity-norm ( i.e., maximum absolute row sum), respectively. The last equality holds because 𝐒 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{S}^{(\ell)} is row-normalized by the softmax function, yielding ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ ∞ = 1 \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{\infty}=1 . Note that this relaxation remains tight, given that attention scores are often concentrated on a few popular items ( cf. Figure 3 ). Nonetheless, this surrogate bound is non-differentiable due to the max operation inherent in the 1-norm. To enable gradient-based optimization, we derive a smooth upper bound for the max operation utilizing the logsumexp function: (4.3) ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ 1 ≤ ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ ~ 1 ≜ 1 τ ​ log ​ ∑ u , t exp ⁡ ( τ ⋅ ‖ 𝐒 u , t ( ℓ ) ‖ 1 ) , \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{1}\leq\widetilde{\|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|}_{1}\triangleq\frac{1}{\tau}\log\sum_{u,t}\exp\left(\tau\cdot\|\mathbf{S}_{u,t}^{(\ell)}\|_{1}\right), where 𝐒 u , t ( ℓ ) \mathbf{S}_{u,t}^{(\ell)} denotes the t t -th column vector of the attention block 𝐒 u ( ℓ ) \mathbf{S}_{u}^{(\ell)} for user u u , and τ \tau is the temperature hyperparameter. As τ → + ∞ \tau\to+\infty , ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ ~ 1 \widetilde{\|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|}_{1} converges to the exact 1-norm ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ 1 \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{1} . In this work, we simply set τ = 1 \tau=1 to eliminate the need for hyperparameter tuning. Optimizing the surrogate objective in ( 4.3 ) offers two compelling advantages: (i) Computational Efficiency : Calculating the matrix 1-norm only requires summing the columns, reducing the time complexity to O ⁡ ( | 𝒰 | ​ n ¯ 2 ) O(|\mathcal{U}|\bar{n}^{2}) and circumventing time-consuming and gradient-unstable SVD operations. (ii) Intuitive Interpretability : The column sums of the attention scores directly reflect the overall influence of each item during aggregation. By constraining the maximum column sum, we effectively prevent the model from over-relying on a few highly popular items ( cf. Section 3.2 ). Finally, one might question why we do not use an alternative surrogate such as the Frobenius norm ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ F \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{F} . Note that ‖ 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ‖ F 2 = ∑ k σ k 2 ​ ( 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ) \|\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}^{2}(\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}) , blindly penalizing the Frobenius norm could simultaneously suppress the remaining singular values σ k ≥ 2 ​ ( 𝐒 ( ℓ ) ) \sigma_{k\geq 2}(\mathbf{S}^{(\ell)}) , resulting in the underutilization of critical long-tail features. Feed-forward Regularization. Another core component that contributes to spectral collapse is the feed-forward projection, where stacking more FFNs can lead to disproportionately faster growth of the spectral norm, as elaborated in Lemma 3.3 . To overcome this issue, inspired by prior works on spectral regularization ( Yoshida and Miyato, 2017 ; Miyato et al., 2018 ; Liu et al., 2019 ) , we propose to penalize the spectral norm of each weight matrix 𝐖 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)} , thereby constraining the overall spectral norm of the feed-forward projection through the following upper bound: (4.4) ∥ 𝐖 ( 1 ) 𝐖 ( 2 ) ⋯ 𝐖 ( L ) ∥ 2 ≤ ∏ ℓ = 1 L ∥ 𝐖 ( ℓ ) ∥ 2 , \|\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\cdots\mathbf{W}^{(L)}\|_{2}\leq\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\|\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}, where ‖ 𝐖 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\|_{2} can be efficiently estimated via the power iteration ( Golub and Van Loan, 2013 ; Golub and Van der Vorst, 2000 ; Yoshida and Miyato, 2017 ) with a time complexity of O ⁡ ( d 2 ) O(d^{2}) for each layer ℓ \ell . Note that each feed-forward projection 𝐖 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)} may consist of multiple linear layers, e.g., 𝐖 ( ℓ ) = 𝐖 1 ( ℓ ) ​ 𝐖 2 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{W}_{1}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}_{2}^{(\ell)} . For ease of implementation, we can further relax the bound to ‖ 𝐖 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 ≤ ‖ 𝐖 1 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 ⋅ ‖ 𝐖 2 ( ℓ ) ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{W}_{1}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}^{(\ell)}\|_{2} , opting to regularize the spectral norm of each projection matrix individually. This upper-bound relationship also holds for architectures with non-linear activations up to a constant factor, since common activation functions ( e.g., ReLU) typically possess a finite Lipschitz constant ( Yoshida and Miyato, 2017 ) . By applying this feed-forward regularization, we effectively curb the risk of spectral norm explosion as depth increases, thereby alleviating the spectral collapse issue. Overall Objective. sections.heading: 4.2. Analyses and Discussions
sections.text: Theoretical Guarantees. To theoretically verify the effectiveness of our method, we establish the following upper-bound relationship between the spectral norm of model predictions and our proposed SPRINT objective ( 4.5 ) to provide a rigorous guarantee for spectral norm control and popularity bias mitigation: Theorem 4.1 . ( Theoretical Guarantee of SPRINT ). With proper hyperparameters λ attn \lambda_{\text{attn}} and λ ffn \lambda_{\text{ffn}} , the SPRINT regularization terms establish a rigorous upper bound on the spectral norm ‖ 𝐘 ^ ‖ 2 \|\hat{\mathbf{Y}}\|_{2} of the final model predictions. The proof is provided in Section A.3 . Theorem 4.1 ensures that minimizing the regularizers in SPRINT effectively constrains the spectral norm of model predictions, thereby providing a theoretical guarantee for mitigating popularity bias ( cf. Lemma 3.1 ). Computational Efficiency. SPRINT is highly computationally efficient. Specifically, the attention regularization merely involves calculating the column sums of the already-computed attention scores, while the feed-forward regularization is efficiently estimated via the power iteration method 3 3 3 Following prior works ( Yoshida and Miyato, 2017 ; Miyato et al., 2018 ) , we do only one power iteration step per forward pass. at each layer. Consequently, the additional time complexity incurred by SPRINT is O ⁡ ( L ​ | 𝒰 | ​ n ¯ 2 + L ​ d 2 ) O(L|\mathcal{U}|\bar{n}^{2}+Ld^{2}) , which is negligible compared to the overall forward and backward passes. Empirically, as illustrated in Figure 7 , we observe that SPRINT incurs only about 3% additional training time. This overhead is highly acceptable given the substantial improvements in both recommendation accuracy and fairness. Discussions on CF Methods. Existing methods in traditional collaborative filtering (CF) have explored mitigating popularity bias by regularizing the spectral norm, which conceptually aligns with our motivation. For instance, ReSN ( Lin et al., 2025 ) proposes to approximate and penalize the spectral norm by factorizing it based on user and item embeddings; LogDet ( Zhang et al., 2023b ) applies redundancy decorrelation regularization to user/item covariance matrices to mitigate embedding collapse in graph-based CF. While these methods achieve promising results in CF scenarios, directly adapting them to sequential recommendation presents two fundamental limitations: (i) They typically rely on static user embeddings. However, in sequential recommendation, user preferences are dynamic and can evolve drastically over time, which renders the optimization of global spectral penalties highly unstable. (ii) They treat the model as a black box and fail to address the unique mechanisms of the transformer architecture, where spectral collapse is inherently exacerbated by the deep stacking of attention and feed-forward layers. In contrast, SPRINT adopts a targeted, layer-wise regularization strategy that explicitly bounds the spectral norm within the specific components responsible for the collapse, thereby enabling stable and highly effective optimization for deep sequential recommenders. sections.heading: 5. Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we conduct extensive experiments to answer the following research questions (RQs): • RQ1 : How does SPRINT perform compared to existing methods in terms of recommendation accuracy and fairness? • RQ2 : How does SPRINT perform under different model scales, especially when stacking more transformer layers? • RQ3 : How do the attention and feed-forward regularizations contribute to the overall performance of SPRINT? • RQ4 : Can SPRINT generalize to other recommendation scenarios, e.g., generative recommendation?

sections.heading: 5.1. Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. To ensure a fair comparison, we conduct experiments on six widely used datasets from MovieLens ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) and Amazon ( He and McAuley, 2016 ; McAuley et al., 2015 ) , specifically including ML-1M/20M, Beauty, Toy, Electronic, Clothing, and Book. The dataset preprocessing strictly follows the previous studies ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) ; further details are provided in Section B.1 . Recommendation Backbones. We evaluate each method on two advanced transformer-based sequential recommendation backbones, namely SASRec++ ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) (2024) and HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) (2024). In the main experiments, we scale the number of layers up to 8 and the embedding dimensionality up to 256. These scale settings deliberately exceed the typical configurations used in prior studies, allowing us to better assess the scalability of different methods. Furthermore, we conduct large-scale experiments on the ML-20M dataset using SASRec++ with up to 0.34B non-embedding parameters (12 layers and 1536-dimensional embeddings), as illustrated in Figure 1 . Please refer to Section B.2 for complete backbone details. Compared Methods. To validate the effectiveness of SPRINT, we compare it against a diverse set of representative debiasing methods from the following categories: (i) spectral regularization , e.g., LogDet ( Zhang et al., 2023b ) (NeurIPS ’23) and ReSN ( Lin et al., 2025 ) (WSDM ’25); (ii) propensity reweighting , e.g., R 2 Rec ( Li et al., 2025 ) (WWW ’25) and D 2 LR ( Lu et al., 2025 ) (SIGIR ’25); (iii) temporal-aware disentanglement , e.g., MOJITO ( Tran et al., 2023 ) (SIGIR ’23) and TPAB ( Yoo et al., 2025 ) (KDD ’25); and (iv) distributionally robust optimization , e.g., DROS ( Yang et al., 2023 ) (SIGIR ’23). We closely follow the original implementations and settings of these methods, adapting them to the sequential recommendation scenario when necessary. Detailed implementations and hyperparameter configurations are provided in Section B.3 . Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate recommendation performance from the perspectives of both accuracy and fairness. For accuracy, we report the widely used NDCG@ K K and HitRatio@ K K metrics, where K ∈ { 5 , 10 } K\in\{5,10\} . For fairness, we mainly adopt the Fairness metric Fair- α \alpha ( Lin et al., 2025 ) measuring the exposure ratio of bottom- α \alpha long-tail items ( α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 in the main experiments, cf. Section 2.2 ). Refer to Table 8 for additional fairness metrics and results.

sections.heading: 5.2. Experimental Results
sections.text: (RQ1) Overall Performance. Tables 1 and 6 present the overall recommendation performance comparison between SPRINT and the baseline methods on the SASRec++ and HSTU backbones. As revealed, SPRINT consistently outperforms all compared methods across all six datasets, yielding an average improvement of +15.70% in NDCG/HR@5 and +7.12% in Fair-0.8. Furthermore, as illustrated in Figure 5 , SPRINT establishes a strictly superior Pareto frontier in the accuracy-fairness trade-off compared to all baselines. This clearly demonstrates the superiority of SPRINT in simultaneously enhancing recommendation quality and mitigating popularity bias. Table 8 reports results on additional fairness metrics. (RQ2) Layer Scaling Performance. As theoretically revealed in Section 3.2 , the popularity bias amplification induced by spectral collapse becomes increasingly severe as more layers are stacked, fundamentally bottlenecking scalability. To examine the effectiveness of SPRINT within deep transformer architectures, we conduct layer-scaling experiments, the results of which are depicted in Figure 4 and Figure 8 . The results demonstrate that our method consistently achieves better accuracy and improved fairness as the model deepens. In contrast, the performance of baseline methods typically stagnates or even degrades due to the unconstrained amplification of popularity bias. This empirical observation perfectly coincides with our discussion in Section 4.2 : the targeted, layer-wise regularization design of SPRINT effectively curbs spectral collapse in deep networks, thereby unlocking sustainable scalability. (RQ3) Ablation Study and Hyperparameter Sensitivity. As shown in Table 7 , both the attention and feed-forward regularizations contribute substantially to the overall performance of SPRINT, with the optimal results achieved when both regularizations are jointly applied. We further analyze the sensitivity of SPRINT to its key hyperparameters, λ attn \lambda_{\text{attn}} and λ ffn \lambda_{\text{ffn}} , which control the strength of the respective regularizations. Results in Figure 9 exhibit a clear performance peak, highlighting the dynamic trade-off between accuracy and fairness. Notably, SPRINT remains highly robust across a reasonably wide range of hyperparameter values, facilitating its practical deployment without the need for exhaustive fine-tuning. (RQ4) Generalization to Generative Recommendation. Finally, we extend SPRINT to the emerging paradigm of generative recommendation, where each item is represented by a unique sequence of semantic IDs. Specifically, we adopt the widely recognized TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) and LETTER ( Wang et al., 2024c ) models as our backbones, and seamlessly apply SPRINT to regularize the self-attention and feed-forward blocks within their underlying T5 ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) architectures. sections.heading: 6. Related Work
sections.text: Sequential Recommendation. Sequential recommendation ( Chang et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2018 ) , which aims to model dynamic user preferences and temporal dependencies in user-item interactions, has long been a fundamental research topic in recommender systems. Early works in this area primarily focus on leveraging RNNs ( Hidasi et al., 2015 ) or CNNs ( Tang and Wang, 2018 ) to capture sequential patterns. With the advent of the attention mechanism ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , transformer-based models ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ) have become the dominant paradigm in sequential recommendation due to their superior capability in modeling long-range dependencies and facilitating parallel computation. In recent years, by aggressively scaling model sizes to billions of parameters ( Zhai et al., 2024 ; Zivic et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Chai et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , the capabilities of sequential recommenders have been significantly advanced, achieving remarkable improvements in recommendation quality. However, while these scaling efforts yield substantial performance gains, they inherently exacerbate popularity bias. This severe side effect has been largely overlooked in the literature, and our work precisely aims to fill this critical gap. Popularity Bias and Debiasing. In recommender systems, popularity bias refers to the notorious phenomenon where popular items are recommended disproportionately more frequently than niche ones, inevitably leading to unfairness and reduced diversity ( Chen et al., 2023 ) . Several lines of research have explored the causes of this bias, attributing it to confounding causal factors ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Wei et al., 2021 ) , long-tail data distributions ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) , and low-rank embedding spaces ( Ohsaka and Togashi, 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ) . Given its detrimental impacts, various debiasing strategies have been proposed. One prominent approach utilizes causal inference techniques to disentangle popularity bias from genuine user preferences ( Ding et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yoo et al., 2025 ) . Yet, these methods typically require carefully crafted causal graphs, which are difficult to generalize across diverse scenarios. Another major direction involves propensity-based reweighting ( Gruson et al., 2019 ; Zhang and Shen, 2023 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , which estimates the propensity scores of items to reweight training samples. However, blindly penalizing popular signals can easily result in suboptimal performance. Other efforts address popularity distribution shifts via temporal-aware modeling ( Tran et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) ; unfortunately, they merely capture the temporal dynamics of the bias without tackling its amplification. Recently, regularization-based methods focusing on decorrelation and spectral collapse ( Zhu et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Lin et al., 2025 ) have been proposed to constrain the optimization trajectory toward more balanced solutions, achieving promising results in standard collaborative filtering. Nonetheless, directly adapting these techniques to sequential recommendation is highly non-trivial due to the unique bias amplification mechanisms inherent in deep transformer architectures. Our work bridges this gap by rigorously analyzing the underlying architectural causes of this amplification and introducing a layer-wise regularization framework to effectively mitigate the issue, thereby unlocking sustainable scalability for deep sequential recommenders.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion and Future Directions
sections.text: This work identifies a critical pitfall in scaling transformer-based sequential recommenders: although increasing model size generally improves recommendation accuracy, it simultaneously amplifies popularity bias. Our theoretical and empirical analyses reveal that this phenomenon is fundamentally rooted in the spectral collapse induced by stacking more attention and feed-forward layers within the transformer. To address this issue, we propose SPRINT, a simple yet effective regularization framework that constrains the maximum column sums of the attention matrix alongside the spectral norms of the feed-forward parameters. Theoretical analysis guarantees that SPRINT effectively curbs popularity bias by strictly upper-bounding the overall spectral norm of model predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPRINT consistently outperforms various representative baselines in terms of both accuracy and fairness. Crucially, SPRINT yields significantly more favorable scaling behaviors, achieving superior accuracy scaling while maintaining a balanced popularity distribution. Looking forward, exploring more computationally efficient implementations of SPRINT ( e.g., integrating it with state-of-the-art efficient attention mechanisms like FlashAttention ( Dao, 2024 ) ) presents a highly promising direction. Furthermore, it would be intriguing to investigate how other scaling dimensions ( e.g., the number of attention heads, embedding dimensionality, and training data volume) intricately impact the recommendation fairness. sections.text: To prove Theorem 3.2 , we first present two lemmas establishing the stability of the spectral norm and singular vectors under perturbations. Lemma A.1 . sections.heading: A.2. Justification of Assumption in Theorem 3.2
sections.text: In Theorem 3.2 , we assume that the left and right principal singular vectors 𝐮 1 \mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} of the attention score matrix 𝐒 \mathbf{S} are highly aligned (omitting the layer index for brevity). Empirically, we verify this assumption by assessing the cosine similarity cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) \cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1}) across different layers. As illustrated in Table 3 , this consistently reveals a high alignment, with cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) \cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1}) ranging between 0.8 and 0.9. Beyond empirical verification, we can also provide a theoretical justification for this assumption in the specific yet representative case, where each diagonal block 𝐒 u \mathbf{S}_{u} of the attention score matrix 𝐒 \mathbf{S} in each layer takes the form of a Cesàro matrix ( Brown et al., 1965 ; Ross, 2022 ) , representing a common autoregressive attention pattern in practice. Formally, a matrix 𝐌 ∈ ℝ m × m \mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is defined as a Cesàro matrix if: (A.28) 𝐌 i , j = { 1 i , if ​ j ≤ i , 0 , otherwise . \mathbf{M}_{i,j}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{i},&\text{if }j\leq i,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} In the context of attention mechanisms, a Cesàro matrix can be interpreted as an attention score matrix where each token attends uniformly to all preceding tokens, which naturally leads to higher attention scores for popular items in sequential recommendation scenarios. For such a matrix 𝐌 \mathbf{M} , we establish the following theorem: Theorem A.3 . Let 𝐌 ∈ ℝ m × m \mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} be a Cesàro matrix, and let 𝐮 1 \mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} denote the principal left and right singular vectors of 𝐌 \mathbf{M} , respectively. Then, we have: (A.29) lim m → ∞ cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) = 1 , \lim_{m\to\infty}\cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})=1, where θ ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \theta(\cdot,\cdot) denotes the angle between two vectors. Proof of Theorem A.3 . To calculate the cosine similarity between the principal left and right singular vectors 𝐮 1 \mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} of the Cesàro matrix 𝐌 \mathbf{M} , we first express 𝐮 1 \mathbf{u}_{1} in terms of 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} . By the definition of the SVD, we have 𝐌 ⊤ ​ 𝐮 1 = σ 1 ​ 𝐯 1 \mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{1}=\sigma_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} , where σ 1 \sigma_{1} is the largest singular value of 𝐌 \mathbf{M} . Provided 𝐌 \mathbf{M} is invertible, we can write 𝐮 1 = σ 1 ​ ( 𝐌 − 1 ) ⊤ ​ 𝐯 1 \mathbf{u}_{1}=\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{M}^{-1})^{\top}\mathbf{v}_{1} , where the inverse 𝐌 − 1 \mathbf{M}^{-1} can be computed explicitly as follows: (A.30) 𝐌 i , j − 1 = { i , j = i , − ( i − 1 ) , j = i − 1 , 0 , otherwise . \mathbf{M}^{-1}_{i,j}=\begin{cases}i,&j=i,\\ -(i-1),&j=i-1,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The cosine similarity cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) = 𝐯 1 ⊤ ​ 𝐮 1 \cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})=\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{1} can then be formulated as a quadratic form of 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} : (A.31) 1 σ 1 ​ cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) = 𝐯 1 ⊤ ​ ( 𝐌 − 1 ) ⊤ ​ 𝐯 1 . \frac{1}{\sigma_{1}}\cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})=\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}(\mathbf{M}^{-1})^{\top}\mathbf{v}_{1}. For simplicity, let v i v_{i} denote the i i -th element of 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} . We can expand this quadratic form as: (A.32) 1 σ 1 ​ cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) = ∑ i = 1 m − 1 i ⁡ ( v i − v i + 1 ) ​ v i + m ​ v m 2 . \frac{1}{\sigma_{1}}\cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}i(v_{i}-v_{i+1})v_{i}+mv_{m}^{2}. Finally, it has been established that the largest singular value σ 1 \sigma_{1} of the Cesàro matrix 𝐌 \mathbf{M} approaches 2 as m → ∞ m\to\infty ( cf. Theorem 5.1 in ( Ross, 2022 ) ). Therefore, taking the limit yields: (A.36) lim m → ∞ cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) = 1 , \lim_{m\to\infty}\cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})=1, which completes the proof. ∎ Building upon Theorem A.3 , we further generalize this result to the sparse block-diagonal case, where the global attention score matrix 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is block-diagonal with each block being a Cesàro matrix. This directly mirrors the practical scenario in sequential recommendation, where the interactions of different users are processed independently. By combining Theorem A.3 and the following Corollary A.4 , we can theoretically justify our assumption in Theorem 3.2 that the principal left and right singular vectors of the attention score matrix are highly aligned across different layers in practice. Corollary A.4 . Let 𝐒 = diag ⁡ ( 𝐒 u ) u ∈ 𝒰 ∈ ℝ N × N \mathbf{S}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{S}_{u})_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} be a block-diagonal attention matrix, where each block 𝐒 u ∈ ℝ n u × n u \mathbf{S}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}\times n_{u}} is a Cesàro matrix representing the causal uniform attention of user u u . Let 𝐮 1 \mathbf{u}_{1} and 𝐯 1 \mathbf{v}_{1} be any pair of corresponding principal left and right singular vectors of the global matrix 𝐒 \mathbf{S} . Then, we have: (A.37) cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) ≥ σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 ) 2 . \cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})\geq\frac{\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S})}{2}. Furthermore, as the maximum sequence length n max = max u ∈ 𝒰 ⁡ n u → ∞ n_{\max}=\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}}n_{u}\to\infty , we have lim n max → ∞ cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 , 𝐯 1 ) = 1 \lim_{n_{\max}\to\infty}\cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1})=1 . Proof of Corollary A.4 . For any user u u , let 𝐮 i ( u ) ∈ ℝ n u \mathbf{u}_{i}^{(u)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}} and 𝐯 i ( u ) ∈ ℝ n u \mathbf{v}_{i}^{(u)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}} denote the i i -th left and right singular vectors of the block 𝐒 u \mathbf{S}_{u} , respectively, for i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n u i=1,2,\cdots,n_{u} . The corresponding singular values are denoted as σ i ​ ( 𝐒 u ) \sigma_{i}(\mathbf{S}_{u}) . We pad these local singular vectors with zeros to match the global dimension N N while maintaining their original coordinates within the block-diagonal structure, resulting in 𝐮 ~ i ( u ) ∈ ℝ N \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}^{(u)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and 𝐯 ~ i ( u ) ∈ ℝ N \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(u)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} . Clearly, 𝐮 ~ i ( u ) \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}^{(u)} and 𝐯 ~ i ( u ) \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(u)} are the left and right singular vectors of the global matrix 𝐒 \mathbf{S} corresponding to the same singular value σ i ​ ( 𝐒 u ) \sigma_{i}(\mathbf{S}_{u}) . Furthermore, the union of all block singular values { σ i ( 𝐒 u ) : u ∈ 𝒰 , i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n u } \{\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{S}_{u}):u\in\mathcal{U},i=1,2,\cdots,n_{u}\} constitutes the entire singular value spectrum of 𝐒 \mathbf{S} . Therefore, the global maximum singular value σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 ) \sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S}) must be achieved by at least one of the block singular values, i.e., σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 ) = max u ∈ 𝒰 ⁡ σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 u ) \sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S})=\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S}_{u}) . Since each block 𝐒 u \mathbf{S}_{u} is a Cesàro matrix, we can apply Theorem A.3 to obtain the following local bound for each user block: (A.38) cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 ~ 1 ( u ) , 𝐯 ~ 1 ( u ) ) = cos ⁡ θ ⁡ ( 𝐮 1 ( u ) , 𝐯 1 ( u ) ) ≥ σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 u ) 2 . \cos\theta(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{1}^{(u)},\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}^{(u)})=\cos\theta(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{(u)},\mathbf{v}_{1}^{(u)})\geq\frac{\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S}_{u})}{2}. Therefore, if there is a unique dominant block that achieves the global maximum singular value σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 ) \sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S}) , then the corresponding zero-padded principal singular vectors of this block are also global, and their cosine similarity is directly lower-bounded by σ 1 ​ ( 𝐒 ) / 2 \sigma_{1}(\mathbf{S})/2 , establishing the desired bound in ( A.37 ). In the more general case where multiple dominant blocks achieve the same global maximum singular value, we can still establish the identical lower bound. The principal singular space is therefore an r r -dimensional degenerate subspace spanned by the zero-padded principal singular vectors { 𝐮 ~ ( j ) } j = 1 r \{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{r} and { 𝐯 ~ ( j ) } j = 1 r \{\tilde{\mathbf{v}}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{r} of these dominant blocks. sections.heading: A.3. Proof of Theorem 4.1
sections.text: To prove Theorem 4.1 , we first extend our proposed objective in ( 4.5 ) to general transformer architectures, which may include multi-head attention, residual connections, layer normalization, and non-linear activation functions. Notably, our core idea is to establish an upper bound for the spectral norm of the model predictions ( i.e., ‖ 𝐘 ^ ‖ 2 \|\hat{\mathbf{Y}}\|_{2} ) in a backward manner, recursively applying the spectral norm bounds from the output of each layer back to the input. Prediction Layer. We first consider the prediction layer, where the model output 𝐘 ^ \hat{\mathbf{Y}} is generated by the multiplication between the last layer output 𝐗 ( L ) \mathbf{X}^{(L)} and the item embedding matrix 𝐄 \mathbf{E} , i.e., 𝐘 ^ = 𝐗 ( L ) ​ 𝐄 ⊤ \hat{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{X}^{(L)}\mathbf{E}^{\top} . Therefore, we can derive the following spectral norm bound for the final predictions: (A.43) ‖ 𝐘 ^ ‖ 2 ≤ ‖ 𝐗 ( L ) ‖ 2 ⋅ ‖ 𝐄 ‖ 2 , \|\hat{\mathbf{Y}}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{X}^{(L)}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{E}\|_{2}, where the first term ‖ 𝐗 ( L ) ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{X}^{(L)}\|_{2} is the spectral norm of the last layer output, which can be recursively upper-bounded by the spectral norm bounds of each preceding layer. The second term ‖ 𝐄 ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{E}\|_{2} can be regularized analogously to the proposed feed-forward regularization in ( 4.4 ) by the power iteration method and can be viewed as a part of the feed-forward regularization. Residual Connections. Next, we consider residual connections, which are typically added after each attention or feed-forward layer. Formally, this operation can be bounded by: (A.44) ‖ 𝐗 block-res ‖ 2 \displaystyle\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-res}}\|_{2} = ‖ 𝐗 block + 𝐗 block-input ‖ 2 \displaystyle=\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block}}+\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}}\|_{2} ≤ ‖ 𝐗 block ‖ 2 + ‖ 𝐗 block-input ‖ 2 , \displaystyle\leq\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block}}\|_{2}+\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}}\|_{2}, where 𝐗 block \mathbf{X}_{\text{block}} is the output of the attention or feed-forward block, and 𝐗 block-input \mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}} is the input to this block. If we can bound the spectral norm of 𝐗 block \mathbf{X}_{\text{block}} by ‖ 𝐗 block ‖ 2 ≤ C block ⋅ ‖ 𝐗 block-input ‖ 2 \|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block}}\|_{2}\leq C_{\text{block}}\cdot\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}}\|_{2} for some scalar amplification factor C block > 0 C_{\text{block}}>0 , then we can bound the spectral norm of the residual output 𝐗 block-res \mathbf{X}_{\text{block-res}} by: (A.45) ‖ 𝐗 block-res ‖ 2 ≤ ( 1 + C block ) ⋅ ‖ 𝐗 block-input ‖ 2 . \|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-res}}\|_{2}\leq(1+C_{\text{block}})\cdot\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}}\|_{2}. Thus, the residual connection can simply be viewed as introducing a multiplicative factor of ( 1 + C block ) (1+C_{\text{block}}) , as opposed to C block C_{\text{block}} in the non-residual case presented in the main text. Consequently, residual connections do not alter the overall form of the spectral norm bound. Our goal then reduces to bounding the spectral norm amplification factor C block C_{\text{block}} of the individual attention and feed-forward blocks, which is precisely achieved by our proposed regularizations. Layer normalization is typically applied prior to the attention and feed-forward blocks ( i.e., pre-norm). In this work, we specifically consider RMSNorm ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) , which generally exhibits better performance than the original LayerNorm with a bias term. Formally, the RMSNorm operation is defined as follows: (A.46) 𝐗 block-norm = 𝐗 block-input-RMS × diag ⁡ ( γ block ) , \mathbf{X}_{\text{block-norm}}=\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input-RMS}}\times\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{\gamma}_{\text{block}}), where 𝐗 block-input-RMS \mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input-RMS}} is the root-mean-square normalized representation obtained from the original input 𝐗 block-input \mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}} , and γ block \mathbf{\gamma}_{\text{block}} is the learnable scaling parameter. To ensure numerical stability, we assume that the minimum 2-norm of the row vectors in any 𝐗 block-input \mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}} is lower-bounded by a positive constant ξ r \xi_{r} , and the maximum absolute value of any element in γ block \mathbf{\gamma}_{\text{block}} is upper-bounded by a positive constant ξ γ \xi_{\gamma} . We can then derive the following spectral norm bound for the layer normalization operation: (A.47) ‖ 𝐗 block-norm ‖ 2 ≤ ξ γ ξ r ​ ‖ 𝐗 block-input ‖ 2 . \|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-norm}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\xi_{\gamma}}{\xi_{r}}\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{block-input}}\|_{2}. Feed-forward Network. Following the standard transformer architecture, we consider a two-layer feed-forward network with a non-linear activation function σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) , i.e., 𝐗 ffn = σ ⁡ ( 𝐗 ffn-norm ​ 𝐖 1 ) ​ 𝐖 2 \mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn}}=\sigma(\mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn-norm}}\mathbf{W}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2} . We assume that the activation function σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is Lipschitz continuous with a finite Lipschitz constant L σ L_{\sigma} , and σ ⁡ ( 𝟎 ) = 𝟎 \sigma(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0} . For instance, the ReLU activation satisfies this assumption with L σ = 1 L_{\sigma}=1 . Then, we establish the spectral norm bound for the feed-forward block: (A.48) ‖ 𝐗 ffn ‖ 2 \displaystyle\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn}}\|_{2} ≤ ‖ σ ⁡ ( 𝐗 ffn-norm ​ 𝐖 1 ) ‖ 2 ⋅ ‖ 𝐖 2 ‖ 2 \displaystyle\leq\|\sigma(\mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn-norm}}\mathbf{W}_{1})\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2} ≤ L σ ​ d ​ ‖ 𝐗 ffn-norm ​ 𝐖 1 ‖ 2 ⋅ ‖ 𝐖 2 ‖ 2 \displaystyle\leq L_{\sigma}\sqrt{d}\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn-norm}}\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2} ≤ L σ ​ d ​ ‖ 𝐖 1 ‖ 2 ​ ‖ 𝐖 2 ‖ 2 ⋅ ‖ 𝐗 ffn-norm ‖ 2 , \displaystyle\leq L_{\sigma}\sqrt{d}\|\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn-norm}}\|_{2}, where the second inequality relies on the spectral norm bound for element-wise operations, i.e., ∥ σ ( ⋅ ) ∥ 2 ≤ ∥ σ ( ⋅ ) ∥ F ≤ L σ ∥ ⋅ ∥ F ≤ L σ d ∥ ⋅ ∥ 2 \|\sigma(\cdot)\|_{2}\leq\|\sigma(\cdot)\|_{F}\leq L_{\sigma}\|\cdot\|_{F}\leq L_{\sigma}\sqrt{d}\|\cdot\|_{2} . The input term 𝐗 ffn-norm \mathbf{X}_{\text{ffn-norm}} can be recursively upper-bounded. Note that the coefficient L σ ​ d L_{\sigma}\sqrt{d} is a constant for a given model architecture, which can be absorbed into the aforementioned ξ γ ξ r \frac{\xi_{\gamma}}{\xi_{r}} term from the layer normalization. Consequently, the entire feed-forward block possesses the following spectral norm amplification factor C ffn C_{\text{ffn}} : (A.49) C ffn = ξ γ ξ r ​ L σ ​ d ​ ‖ 𝐖 1 ‖ 2 ​ ‖ 𝐖 2 ‖ 2 , C_{\text{ffn}}=\frac{\xi_{\gamma}}{\xi_{r}}L_{\sigma}\sqrt{d}\|\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2}, which perfectly aligns with our proposed feed-forward regularization in ( 4.4 ) up to a constant multiplier. sections.heading: B.1. Datasets
sections.text: To ensure a fair comparison with existing methods, we conduct experiments on six widely used benchmark datasets from MovieLens ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) and Amazon ( He and McAuley, 2016 ; McAuley et al., 2015 ) , specifically including ML-1M/20M, Beauty, Toy, Electronic, Clothing, and Book. The dataset preprocessing strictly follows the standard procedure from previous studies ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , where users and items with fewer than 5 interactions are filtered out ( i.e., 5-core), and the remaining interactions are sorted in chronological order. For each user, the most recent interaction is used for testing, the second most recent interaction is used for validation, and all remaining historical interactions are used for training ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, following the common practice in sequential recommendation ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ) , the historical interaction sequences for each user are truncated to a maximum length of 200 on ML-1M/20M and 50 on the Amazon datasets. Detailed statistics of the datasets are summarized in Table 4 .

sections.heading: B.2. Backbones
sections.text: We evaluate each method on two advanced transformer-based sequential recommendation backbones, namely SASRec++ ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) (2024) and HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) (2024). The former adapts SASRec ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ) with several architectural adjustments for better scalability, while the latter modifies the attention mechanism to increase model capacity and improve computational efficiency. In our main experiments, we scale the number of layers up to 8 and the embedding dimensionality up to 256. These scale settings deliberately exceed the typical configurations used in prior studies, allowing us to better assess the scalability of different methods. Furthermore, we conduct large-scale experiments on the ML-20M dataset using SASRec++ with up to 0.34B non-embedding parameters (12 layers and 1536-dimensional embeddings), as illustrated in Figure 1 . The backbone details are provided below: SASRec++ ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) . Kang and McAuley (2018) initially proposed the SASRec architecture, which consists of a stack of transformer blocks. As model sizes scaled up, Zhang et al. (2024b) and Guo et al. (2024) identified several architectural bottlenecks in the original design and proposed a series of adjustments to enhance scalability. Following these works, we adopt the improved SASRec++ architecture as one of our evaluation backbones. SASRec++ directly utilizes the standard LlamaDecoder architecture ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) , incorporating pre-norm LayerNorm, RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) for positional encoding, an intermediate dimensionality of 4 ​ d 4d for the feed-forward network, and optional dropout on the attention weights. In the main experiments, the number of attention heads is searched over { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{1,2,4,8\} for different layer configurations, while it is fixed to d / 64 d/64 for the large-scale experiments on ML-20M. Specifically, for the layer scaling experiments, we fix the embedding dimensionality to 512 and vary the number of layers. Detailed architectural configurations for the large-scale experiments are provided in Table 5 . HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) . HSTU is a recently proposed backbone that achieves state-of-the-art performance in industrial-scale sequential recommendation. The core modification of HSTU is the introduction of a SiLU-based attention mechanism, which replaces the traditional softmax function with the SiLU activation to compute attention scores. In this work, we generalize the original HSTU architecture to support an optional feed-forward network (which is absent in the original HSTU) and an optional gated attention mechanism (which is present in the original HSTU). Empirically, we observe that in certain settings, incorporating the feed-forward network and removing the gated attention can further improve training stability and performance. To ensure a fair comparison, all experiments on the HSTU backbone are conducted by searching over these feed-forward and gated attention options, and we report the best results for each method. Training Details. For all evaluated methods, we adopt the Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ) with negative sampling as the main recommendation loss in ( 4.5 ), where the number of negative samples is set to 32 for ML-1M/20M and 16 for Amazon datasets. We utilize the AdamW optimizer ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} and a weight decay of 0.1 0.1 in our main experiments. The warmup ratio is set to 0.05 0.05 , after which the learning rate is linearly decayed to zero. For the large-scale experiments on the ML-20M dataset, we search over learning rates in { 10 − 3 , 5 × 10 − 4 , 10 − 4 } \{10^{-3},5\times 10^{-4},10^{-4}\} and weight decays in { 0.1 , 0.01 } \{0.1,0.01\} to ensure stable training. The batch size is fixed at 512 for main experiments and 1024 for large-scale experiments, and the maximum number of training epochs is set to 200 across all experiments. The optimal results for all methods in the main experiments are selected based on the NDCG@5 metric. The remaining hyperparameters for the compared methods and SPRINT are searched over the ranges specified in Section B.3 . Runtime comparison. Figure 7 . sections.heading: B.3. Compared Methods
sections.text: The details of the compared methods are summarized below: • DROS ( Yang et al., 2023 ) : A distributionally robust optimization (DRO) method that incorporates KL-divergence-based DRO ( Wang et al., 2024a ) regularization, weighted by the item popularity distribution, to enhance model robustness against distribution shifts. Key hyperparameters: temperature β 0 ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 , 1.5 } \beta_{0}\in\{0.5,1.0,1.5\} , weight α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\} . • MOJITO ( Tran et al., 2023 ) : A temporal-aware disentanglement method that separates temporal context and item representations, explicitly disentangling the short-term time-dependent intents from context-independent long-term preferences. Key hyperparameters: weight λ ∈ { 0.01 , 0.1 , 0.5 } \lambda\in\{0.01,0.1,0.5\} . • TPAB ( Yoo et al., 2025 ) : A temporal-aware disentanglement approach that separates intrinsic item property embeddings from temporal-popularity embeddings via exponential time bucketing. Key hyperparameters: number of buckets K ∈ { 20 , 40 , 60 } K\in\{20,40,60\} , bootstrapping weight λ ∈ { 0 , 0.5 , 1.0 , 1.5 , 2.0 , 2.5 , 3.0 } \lambda\in\{0,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0\} . • R 2 Rec ( Li et al., 2025 ) : A propensity reweighting method that incorporates adaptive loss reweighting, coupled with a Gaussian reembedding operation for tail items, to explicitly prioritize tail item optimization. Key hyperparameter: temperature τ ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.5 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.05,0.1,0.5,1.0\} . • D 2 LR ( Lu et al., 2025 ) : A propensity reweighting method that performs token-level inverse propensity score (IPS) debiasing. Key hyperparameters: α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , … , 0.9 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.2,\dots,0.9\} and β ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , … , 0.4 } \beta\in\{0.05,0.1,\dots,0.4\} . • LogDet ( Zhang et al., 2023b ) : A spectral regularization method that mitigates dimensional collapse by regularizing the covariance matrix of item embeddings via log-determinant divergence. Key hyperparameter: weight λ ∈ { 10 − 3 , 10 − 4 , 10 − 5 , 10 − 6 } \lambda\in\{10^{-3},10^{-4},10^{-5},10^{-6}\} . • ReSN ( Lin et al., 2025 ) : A spectral regularization method that constrains the largest singular value of the predicted interaction matrix to mitigate popularity bias. Key hyperparameter: regularization weight λ ∈ { 10 − 3 , 10 − 4 , 10 − 5 , 10 − 6 } \lambda\in\{10^{-3},10^{-4},10^{-5},10^{-6}\} . • SPRINT (Ours) : The proposed method that jointly regularizes the spectral norms of attention and feed-forward components to mitigate the spectral collapse during scaling. Key hyperparameters: attention regularization weight λ attn ∈ { 2.5 , 5.0 , 7.5 , 10 } \lambda_{\text{attn}}\in\{2.5,5.0,7.5,10\} for the main experiments, and λ attn ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 } \lambda_{\text{attn}}\in\{0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5\} for the large-scale experiments on the ML-20M dataset, feed-forward regularization weight λ ffn ∈ { 10 − 1 , 10 − 2 , 10 − 3 , 10 − 4 } \lambda_{\text{ffn}}\in\{10^{-1},10^{-2},10^{-3},10^{-4}\} .

In Figure 6 , we conduct an ablation study to isolate the effects of the attention and feed-forward components on the spectral collapse of model predictions. Specifically, we compare the severity of spectral collapse in the full transformer model against variants where multiple attention blocks or feed-forward blocks are omitted. The results clearly indicate that both components independently contribute to the exacerbation of spectral collapse. Replacing either component with identity mappings ( i.e., removing them) significantly mitigates this collapse. This finding empirically verifies the necessity of jointly regularizing both the attention and feed-forward components to effectively control the spectral collapse inherent in scaling sequential recommenders. Cross-Layer Alignment of Singular Vectors. In Theorem 3.2 , we assume that the singular vectors of the attention score matrices are highly aligned across layers, up to small perturbations. This crucial assumption enables us to derive a closed-form lower bound for the spectral norm of multi-layer attention aggregation. To empirically verify this, we compute the cosine similarity between the singular vectors of the attention score matrices across different layers within a 8-layer trained transformer. Our results reveal that this cross-layer cosine similarity remains consistently high (above 0.7788 on the ML-1M dataset, and above 0.7845 on the Beauty dataset). This evidence empirically verifies the validity of our assumption and confirms the practical applicability of the derived spectral norm bound. We identify a critical pitfall in scaling transformer-based sequential recommenders: while increasing model size improves recommendation accuracy, it simultaneously amplifies popularity bias . This bias drives systems to over-recommend popular items at the expense of niche ones, which not only undermines fairness but also degrades the broader ecosystem by reinforcing the Matthew effect and filter bubbles. Consequently, this bias amplification emerges as a fundamental obstacle to sustainable model scaling. Through comprehensive theoretical and empirical analyses, we uncover the root cause of this amplification. Our findings reveal that as model depth increases, the two core components of the transformer architecture, i.e., attention aggregation and feed-forward projections, synergistically induce severe spectral collapse in model predictions, which directly translates to the amplification of popularity bias. To address this challenge, we propose SPRINT ( S calable P opularity R egularization IN T ransformers), which mitigates spectral collapse during scaling by constraining (i) the maximum column-sums of the attention score matrices and (ii) the spectral norms of the feed-forward parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPRINT significantly improves both accuracy and long-tail fairness. Crucially, it yields more favorable scaling behaviors when expanding model sizes from 0.05M to 0.34B parameters. The code is available at https://github.com/Tiny-Snow/GenRec . Introduction The discovery of scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of modern machine learning. These laws characterize a remarkable empirical regularity: model performance improves predictably (often following a power law) as the number of parameters or the volume of data increases ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022a ) . Guided by these observations, transformer-based foundation models have been scaled to billions or even trillions of parameters ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025a ) , unlocking unprecedented proficiency in contextual understanding ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Hao et al., 2025 ) , complex reasoning ( Wei et al., 2022b ; Wang et al., 2025c ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , and agency ( Hao et al., 2026a ; Hao et al., 2026b ) . Inspired by this success, researchers have increasingly explored scaling laws in recommender systems, particularly in sequential recommendation ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Recent studies have observed a similar trend: scaling up the parameters of transformer-based sequential recommenders leads to consistent improvements in recommendation accuracy, which has also been validated in large-scale industrial recommender systems ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zivic et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . Movielens-20M scaling laws. Figure 1 . Scaling laws of accuracy (NDCG@5) and fairness (Fair-0.95) on transformer-based sequential recommenders, across (1) different number of non-embedding parameters (0.05M to 0.34B) and (2) different transformer depths (1 to 16 layers). Here we present results on the MovieLens-20M dataset ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) with the advanced SASRec++ backbone ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) , and the fairness metric denotes the ratio of bottom-95% long-tail items exposed in top-1 recommendations. Notably, as model size increases, especially by deepening layers, fairness tends to degrade due to amplified popularity bias. Our proposed SPRINT effectively mitigates this bias, enabling superior scaling performance in both accuracy and fairness. Movielens-20M scaling laws. Challenge. However, we uncover a critical pitfall of scaling sequential recommenders: as model size increases, especially when increasing transformer depth, popularity bias is simultaneously amplified, as shown in Figure 1 . Popularity bias ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) , a notorious issue in recommender systems, denotes the tendency to over-recommend popular items at the expense of niche ones. This bias adversely affects both accuracy and fairness and can further degrade the recommendation ecosystem by reinforcing the Matthew effect and intensifying filter bubbles through the user-system feedback loop ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . The severity of these consequences poses a fundamental challenge to achieving sustainable scaling in recommendation. Analysis. To tackle this challenge, we first conduct theoretical and empirical analyses to pinpoint the root cause behind the amplification of popularity bias during model scaling. Prior work by Lin et al. (2025) indicates that item popularity is primarily encoded within the principal spectral component of the model’s prediction score matrix, which is weighted by the largest singular value ( i.e., the spectral norm) in the singular value decomposition ( cf. Lemma 3.1 ). Based on this insight, we further empirically observe that increasing transformer depth exacerbates spectral collapse ( Jing et al., 2021 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Ohsaka and Togashi, 2023 ) : the largest singular value grows disproportionately dominant relative to the rest of the singular values, thereby magnifying the influence of the popularity-related principal component on final recommendations, and consequently amplifying popularity bias as model scales up ( cf. Figure 1 ). Diving deeper into the architectural mechanisms, we attribute the aforementioned depth-induced spectral collapse to the two core components of transformer-based sequential recommenders: attention aggregation and feed-forward projections . Specifically, the attention mechanism can over-emphasize popular items as they tend to accumulate disproportionately high attention weights. Our theoretical analysis further shows that stacking layers with such popularity-priority attention intensifies spectral collapse by increasing the spectral norm exponentially with depth ( cf. Theorem 3.2 ). Moreover, the gradient dynamics of stacked feed-forward projections can make gradient-based optimization less effective in learning features within the long-tail singular space, further exacerbating spectral collapse as the network deepens ( cf. Lemma 3.3 ). Together, these two mechanisms synergistically amplify popularity bias and impede the scalability of sequential recommenders. Our Method. Given the adverse impact of popularity bias on the fairness and sustainability of recommendation systems, developing effective debiasing strategies is crucial. While numerous debiasing methods have been proposed ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Zhang and Shen, 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ; Ning et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Lin et al., 2025 ) , most primarily target traditional collaborative filtering scenarios, overlooking the unique characteristics of sequential recommendation and the implications of model architectures on scaling laws. Consequently, these approaches are less effective in addressing the popularity bias amplification observed during scaling. To bridge this gap, we propose SPRINT , a popularity regularization method tailored to transformer-based sequential recommenders. Motivated by our prior theoretical analysis, SPRINT introduces two key regularizers: (i) attention regularization , which constrains the maximum column-sums of the attention score matrices, limiting the excessive accumulation of popularity signals during attention aggregation, thus mitigating popularity bias amplification; and (ii) feed-forward regularization , which bounds the spectral norms of the feed-forward projection weights, thereby controlling spectral collapse as depth increases. By regularizing these core components in each layer, SPRINT can natively alleviate spectral collapse when training deeper transformers. SPRINT offers three appealing properties: (i) We prove that SPRINT upper-bounds the spectral norm of the prediction score matrix, providing theoretical guarantees for mitigating popularity bias amplification ( cf. Theorem 4.1 ). (ii) Unlike existing debiasing approaches, SPRINT directly targets the architectural sources of this amplification by regularizing the specific transformer components. (iii) SPRINT is computationally efficient, introducing negligible training overhead. These properties make SPRINT a principled and effective debiasing solution for scaling sequential recommenders. We evaluate SPRINT on six benchmark datasets using two strong sequential recommendation backbones: SASRec++ ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Guo et al., 2024 ) and HSTU ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) . Experimental results demonstrate that SPRINT significantly improves both accuracy (avg. +15.70% in NDCG and HR) and long-tail exposure (avg. +7.12%). To assess scalability, we test model sizes ranging from 0.05M to 0.34B non-embedding parameters (a 6912 × \times scale-up). The results show that SPRINT achieves better accuracy scaling while maintaining a more balanced popularity distribution ( cf. Figure 1 ). We further extend SPRINT to the generative recommendation scenario and observe consistent gains on the state-of-the-art backbones TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) and LETTER ( Wang et al., 2024c ) . Our Contributions • We identify a critical scaling pitfall in sequential recommendation: while accuracy improves with model scaling, popularity bias is simultaneously amplified. • We reveal that attention aggregation and feed-forward projections in transformer synergistically exacerbate the spectral collapse of model predictions, thereby intensifying popularity bias as depth grows. • We propose SPRINT, a principled and effective popularity regularization method that constrains the maximum column-sums of the attention matrices and the spectral norms of feed-forward parameters to mitigate this spectral collapse. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPRINT significantly improves both accuracy and fairness ( i.e., long-tail exposure), yielding more favorable scaling behaviors. 2. Preliminaries In this section, we formulate the sequential recommendation task in Section 2.1 , introduce the popularity bias in Section 2.2 , and present the transformer-based model architectures in Section 2.3 . 2.1. Task Formulation In this work, we focus on sequential recommendation ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2026a ; Cui et al., 2026b ) , a widely adopted paradigm in real-world recommender systems. Formally, given a set of users 𝒰 \mathcal{U} and a set of items ℐ \mathcal{I} , each user u ∈ 𝒰 u\in\mathcal{U} interacts with a sequence of items ( i u , 1 , i u , 2 , ⋯ , i u , n u ) (i_{u,1},i_{u,2},\cdots,i_{u,n_{u}}) in chronological order. Here, i u , t ∈ ℐ i_{u,t}\in\mathcal{I} denotes the t t -th item the user interacts with, and n u n_{u} represents the length of the interaction sequence. Given this historical sequence as input, the goal of a sequential recommendation model is to predict the next item i u , n u + 1 i_{u,n_{u}+1} that the user is most likely to interact with. 2.2. Popularity Bias Recommender systems often exhibit a long-tail distribution of item popularity, where a small fraction of items ( i.e., popular items ) receive a disproportionately large number of interactions, while the majority of items ( i.e., long-tail items ) are rarely interacted with ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . For instance, in the ML-1M dataset ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) , the top-20% of items (ranked by popularity) account for 62.6% of all interactions, while the bottom-40% account for only 5.4%. Such a skewed data distribution poses significant challenges for training effective recommendation models, as these models often amplify this skewness by over-recommending popular items. For example, when employing the state-of-the-art HSTU model ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) on ML-1M, we observe that over 80% of the recommendations are dominated by the top-20% popular items, whereas the bottom-40% long-tail items are recommended less than 1% of the time. This notorious phenomenon, known as popularity bias , not only hinders recommendation accuracy but also leads to information cocoons, inequitable exposure, and reduced user satisfaction ( Zhu et al., 2021 ; Klimashevskaia et al., 2024 ) . To quantify the extent of popularity bias in recommendation systems, we additionally measure a fairness metric Fair- α \alpha , defined as the ratio of bottom- α \alpha long-tail items in the final recommendations, which is also referred to as the long-tail exposure. Following prior work ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate Fair-0.8 by treating the bottom 80% of items as long-tail items across most datasets ( cf. Table 1 ). For the ML-20M dataset, due to its massive scale and particularly skewed popularity distribution, we instead evaluate Fair-0.95 ( cf. Figure 1 ). In the main text, we primarily evaluate fairness in top-1 recommendations, while the similar trends can be observed in top-5 and top-10 recommendations ( cf. Table 8 ). 2.3. Model Architecture Motivated by the widespread success of the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , transformer-based models have gained significant traction and achieved state-of-the-art performance in sequential recommendation ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ) . For ease of exposition, we detail only the single-head attention mechanism and standard two-layer feed-forward networks, purposely omitting auxiliary components like residual connections and layer normalization. Pitfalls of Scaling Laws In this section, we identify a critical pitfall in scaling sequential recommendation models: while scaling up model size generally enhances performance, it simultaneously amplifies popularity bias . We first provide empirical evidence in Section 3.1 , then conduct empirical and theoretical analyses of the root causes in Section 3.2 . 3.1. Popularity Bias Amplification Motivated by recent efforts to scale sequential recommendation models ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zivic et al., 2024 ) , we conduct an empirical study to investigate the impact of model size on both recommendation accuracy and fairness. As shown in Figure 1 .(1), our results reveal an intriguing pattern: while overall recommendation accuracy improves with larger model sizes, recommendation fairness exhibits a non-monotonic trajectory. Specifically, popularity bias decreases as model size grows to a moderate scale ( e.g., 18.9M), likely due to an enhanced capacity to align with user preferences. However, when further scaling to large sizes ( e.g., 0.13B and 0.34B), popularity bias significantly worsens, suggesting an increased tendency to over-recommend popular items and underutilize long-tail features. More crucially, this popularity bias is continuously amplified as model depth increases, eventually becoming a bottleneck to further scaling. In Figure 1 .(2), we observe accuracy saturation, and in some cases even degradation, when model depth is increased ( e.g., over 8 layers) without additional debiasing mechanisms. Overall, these findings reveal a critical pitfall in scaling sequential recommenders: Observation: Popularity Bias Pitfall in Scaling When scaling model size, particularly by increasing model depth, popularity bias is simultaneously amplified and can become a bottleneck to further scaling. 3.2. Analyses on the Root Causes Our observations in Section 3.1 have identified the critical pitfall in scaling transformer-based sequential recommenders, prompting a natural question: what are the root causes of popularity bias amplification during model scaling? Spectral Norm and Popularity Bias. To answer this question, we first revisit the theoretical insights from Lin et al. Spectral norm analysis of layer scaling. Spectral Collapse in Deep Transformers. Building on the above insight, we further analyze how transformer architectures contribute to spectral collapse in model outputs. Here, spectral collapse refers to the phenomenon that the largest singular value of the prediction matrix dominates the singular value spectrum, i.e., σ 1 \sigma_{1} becomes disproportionately large relative to the remaining singular values σ k ≥ 1 \sigma_{k\geq 1} . As a consequence, the principal spectral component, which is closely associated with item popularity, exerts an excessively strong influence on recommendation outcomes. Empirically, in Figure 2 , we observe that spectral collapse consistently intensifies with depth, suggesting that deeper transformer stacks inherently exacerbate this effect and drive bias amplification. To facilitate intuitive understanding and theoretical derivations, we assume identity activations in the feed-forward networks. Methodology Given the aforementioned concerns regarding popularity bias amplification during model scaling, as well as the underlying causes rooted in spectral collapse from stacking attention and feed-forward layers, blindly scaling up sequential recommenders without constraining spectral norm growth will almost inevitably lead to sub-optimal scalability. Motivated by this critical pitfall, we propose SPRINT ( S calable P opularity R egularization IN T ransformers), a principled approach that explicitly bounds the spectral norm within key transformer components to mitigate bias amplification and unlock sustainable scalability. In the following, we first present the algorithmic details of SPRINT in Section 4.1 , and subsequently provide theoretical analyses and comparative discussions in Section 4.2 . 4.1.
